title: Where AI can help a small business—and where a person should stay in control
seoTitle: Where AI Can Help a Small Business
description: Find useful AI opportunities in your business: request summaries, knowledge search and draft replies, with practical checks for accuracy, access and human review.
author: Karol Songin
takeaway: Give AI a defined job with approved inputs and a checkable result. Use a simpler rule when that solves the problem, and keep consequential decisions under appropriate human control.

cta.heading: Your business needs a better flow. Start there.
cta.body: We look at how your business works, identify the bottlenecks and define a first improvement. Then we build the website, dashboard or automation the work actually needs.
cta.label: Explore the business review and build approach

sections.heading: Start with the work, not the technology
sections.body:
“We should use AI” is not yet a business problem. “Someone spends half an hour turning a long customer request into a usable brief” is. The second statement gives you a task, inputs and a result to inspect.

A useful business review asks where work needs interpretation, where information is hard to find and where a draft could help someone move faster. It also asks whether a normal rule, a better form or a direct integration would solve the problem more reliably.

AI is a building option. It should earn its place in the process rather than become the purpose of the project.

sections.heading: Four useful opportunities to investigate
sections.body: These are starting points for a trial, not guarantees. Suitability depends on the information available, access permissions, quality expectations and the cost of an incorrect result.

rows: Prepare a structured summary and list of missing information.
Check the original request before quoting or committing.
Find relevant guidance and present an answer with its source.
Verify important details and handle exceptions.
Prepare a draft using approved wording and record context.
Review before sending where the message needs judgement.
Suggest a category or route for a person to confirm.

sections.heading: Keep fixed rules fixed
sections.body:
If every valid enquiry needs a record, an owner and a task, a normal workflow rule may be enough. You do not need a language model to add a standard reminder or move a known field between systems.

A clear rule is easier to test: given these inputs, expect this result. AI output can vary and needs a different evaluation approach. Use it when interpretation adds value, not merely because the task happens on a computer.

The strongest setup may combine both. AI prepares a draft summary; a person approves it; a deterministic workflow creates the agreed task.

sections.heading: Work through a request-summary example
sections.body:
A customer sends a long message about an installation. It includes a location, preferred dates, access constraints and several questions. An assistant can prepare a draft brief from that message, including points that still need clarification.

The owner sees the original message beside the draft. They check that important details are present and that the summary has not invented missing facts. They then confirm the next action.

If the request is ambiguous, the correct outcome may be asking the customer a question. A confident-looking paragraph is not evidence that the assistant understood everything.

Test examples with conflicting dates, unclear instructions and missing details. Include messages that do not fit the service. Decide what a useful summary looks like before judging the trial.

sections.heading: Access and data handling are part of the design
sections.body:
An assistant should only receive information needed for its agreed job. Consider which records a user is allowed to access and enforce that access in the connected system, rather than relying on the assistant to decide.

Review the provider’s data handling, retention, account settings and relevant agreements before sending customer information. The right arrangement depends on the service and information involved. ICO guidance addresses data protection questions around AI.

Content from messages or documents can contain instructions that attempt to alter an assistant’s behaviour. OWASP describes prompt injection as an application risk. Treat external content as information to process, keep tool actions constrained and check permissions before acting.

sections.heading: Measure whether it helps after review
sections.body:
A fast draft that takes longer to correct has not improved the process. Compare the existing task with the whole assisted workflow, including checking and corrections.

Use a representative set of examples and record the outcomes. Define what counts as an unacceptable error, what requires escalation and what should happen when the provider is unavailable. A useful system needs a fallback as well as a success path.
bullets: Time to reach an approved result, including review.
Important details missed or incorrectly added.
Requests that correctly ask for clarification.
Clear handling of uncertainty and unavailable services.
Usage costs and the effort needed to maintain the setup.

sections.heading: Give the first AI feature a narrow boundary
sections.body:
Start with one checkable task and the people responsible for it. You can learn from that trial without giving an assistant broad authority over customer messages, quotes or payments.

EfiOps can review where AI might help alongside ordinary automation and integration. If it has a useful role, we define the inputs, boundaries, review steps and evaluation criteria before building it into your website or business app.

callout.title: A useful first question
callout.body: Where would a good draft help someone do their job, and who can verify it? That is a stronger starting point than asking an assistant to run the business.
